[{:db/id 17592186231788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.\n\nAs before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as\n\n$$\ny=y_c+y_p,\n$$\n\nwhere $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.\n\nThe main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:\n\n- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then\n\n- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.\n\nWhen $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$\n\nRecall that for an equation of the form $y''+\\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:\n\n- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.\n\n- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.\n\nFor example, consider the boundary value problem\n\n$$\ny''+5y=f(x)\n$$\n\non $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.\n\nBecause $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is\n\n$$\n\\cos\\left(\\dfrac{n\\pi x}{2}\\right)\n\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad\n\\sin\\left(\\dfrac{n\\pi x}{2}\\right).\n$$\n\nNext, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.\n\nTherefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:\n\n$$\ny_p(x)=\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} b_n\\sin\\left(\\dfrac{n\\pi x}{2}\\right).\n$$\n\nLet's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "67a0ca11-7450-5f6a-8bdc-4aee6301f209" [{:db/id 17592186084381 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084509 :tutorial/content "Let $\\triangle{ABC}$ be a triangle where the lengths $AB=7$ and $AC=5$ are fixed. For example, consider the triangle shown below.\n\n![](images/e4/e4c1df256d9a40c50e3535f3055fef041cf02710c0a9e0414acae1bf38681ff4.png)\n\nNow, suppose that we vary the angle $\\angle{A}$, making it either very small or very large. What would be the maximum possible length of the side $\\overline {BC}$ for which the figure is still a triangle?\n\nWe make the longest possible segment $\\overline{BC}$ by increasing the angle $\\angle{A}$ as shown in the sketches below. Here, we fix vertices $A$ and $B$, and then \"rotate\" the side $\\overline{AC}$ about the vertex $A$ until $\\angle{A}$ measures $180^\\circ$.\n\n![](images/d9/d9777d021ad9aac118452b691567d325939c5c8591b777f2cf9c17b39916e660.png)\n\nFrom the picture, we can see that when\n\n$$\nm\\angle{A}=180^\\circ\n$$\n\nwe will not have a triangle anymore and the length of $\\overline{BC}$ will be\n\n$$\n7+5=12\n$$\n\nTherefore, if we would like to have a triangle, $\\overline{BC}$ must be shorter than the sum of the other sides:\n$BC \\mid < AB + AC; < 7 + 5; < 12$\n\nThis is true for all triangles:\n\n> In every triangle, the length of any one side must be smaller than the sum of the other two sides.\n\nThe above statement is one part of the **triangle inequality theorem**, which we will continue building upon in this lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "29fc4755-2259-5126-bad7-5e7c73c355b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8192 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "13ee6ddf-a2c8-5588-8e52-f8a84af5eba4" :step/math-academy-id 73696 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084382}} {:db/id 17592186084382 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083395 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082921 :question/id #uuid "25a73406-c869-5786-af97-cf90866eb1a7" :question/math-academy-id "e-13101"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "768204cd-ee1f-5271-9ec9-71d672b4eb9e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048336}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083834} {:db/id 17592186083835}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Impossible Sides of a Triangle"} :step/id #uuid "a2043004-3f75-55f7-8ceb-e7960310878d" :step/math-academy-id 73697 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084383}} {:db/id 17592186084383 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084510 :tutorial/content "Consider the same triangle as before, with sides $5$ and $7$. This time, what is the shortest possible length of the side $\\overline {BC}$, for which the figure is still a triangle?\n\nWe make the shortest possible segment $\\overline{BC}$ by decreasing the angle $\\angle{A}$. Again, we fix $A$ and $B$, and then \"rotate\" the side $\\overline{AC}$ about the vertex $A$ towards the side $\\overline{AB}$.\n\n![](images/7d/7d1bd3363c2c218c6a2813a957bace3d29b7240919ced63d58be299e9478c099.png)\n\nFrom the picture, we can see that for\n\n$$\nm\\angle{A}=0^\\circ\n$$\n\nwe will not have a triangle anymore and the length of $\\overline{BC}$ will be $7-5=2$. Therefore, if we would like to have a triangle, $\\overline{BC}$ must be longer than the difference of the other sides:\n$BC \\mid > AB - AC; > 7 - 5; > 2$\n\nThis is true for all triangles:\n\n> In every triangle, the length of any one side must be larger than the difference of the other two sides.\n\nThe above statement is the other part of the **triangle inequality theorem**." :tutorial/id #uuid "64f2a60c-c156-5226-a994-9c2f141a59db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8193 :tutorial/title "The Difference of Two Sides"} :step/id #uuid "a2714886-a7e1-52ee-ba1b-b1922a69c5ca" :step/math-academy-id 73700 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084384}} {:db/id 17592186084384 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084511 :tutorial/content "All of the discussion so far can be summarized in the following statement that is called the **triangle inequality theorem**.\n\n> *In a triangle, the length of a side must be greater than the difference of the lengths of the other two sides and less than the sum of those lengths.*\n\nLet's write that down using mathematical notations. Suppose that in a triangle the length of a side equals $a$ and the other two sides have length $b$ and $c$ with $b>c$. Then, we must have\n$b - c < a < b + c$.\n\nIf we would like to omit the assumption that $b>c$, we can still use the same inequality, as long as we include an absolute value on the left-hand side:\n$\\mid b - c \\mid < a < b + c$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cd8d2616-ebae-5d43-89d3-470c89118c36" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8194 :tutorial/title "The Triangle Inequality Theorem"} :step/id #uuid Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}[\\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =-\\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}[\\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{aligned}] \\\\ {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t) & =-\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}12t \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{2t} \\\\ 8t{e}^{-t}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, using our formula for $u(t),$ we (-{e}^{-t})-\\int -{e}^{-t}\\cdot 8\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\\int 8\\,{e}^{-t}\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\\\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our -8{e}^{-t}(1+t)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}(1-2t)-16(1+t) \\\\ 2(1-2t)-8(1+t)\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-18t-15 \\\\ -12t-6\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id equations\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}'(t) =\nA\n\\mathbf{x}(t) +\n\\mathbf{f}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.\n\nIn this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.\n\nRecall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{c}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.\n\nAs usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{u}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.\n\nDifferentiating $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\\,u(t))^{′} \\\\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, since $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, since $\\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\\Phi' = A \\Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, since $\\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\\Phi^{-1}{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\\cdot f(t) \\\\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {u}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our particular solution is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \\Phi \\displaystyle\\int \\Phi^{-1}\\mathbf{f}(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166985} {:db/id 17592186167896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}'(t) =\nA\n\\mathbf{x}(t) +\n\\mathbf{f}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.\n\nIn this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.\n\nRecall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{c}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.\n\nAs usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{u}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.\n\nDifferentiating $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\\,u(t))^{′} \\\\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, since $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, since $\\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\\Phi' = A \\Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, since $\\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\\Phi^{-1}{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\\cdot f(t) \\\\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {u}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our particular solution is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \\Phi \\displaystyle\\int \\Phi^{-1}\\mathbf{f}(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" \n\n$$\n\\{ \\sin x, \\, \\cos x, \\, 2\\sin x \\}\n$$\n\ndefined on $x \\in \\mathbb{R}.$\n\nNotice that for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R},$ we have that\n\n$$\n2 \\cdot \\sin x +\n0 \\cdot \\cos x +\n(-1) \\cdot 2\\sin x = 0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, since not all the scalar coefficients in the linear combination are zero, the given set of functions is linearly dependent.\n\nLet's see another example." :step/next {:db/id 17592186153272}} {:db/id 17592186153272 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153329 :tutorial/content "A **fundamental set of solutions** to a homogeneous, linear differential equation of degree $n$ is a set of precisely $n$ linearly independent solutions.\n\nFor example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation \n\n$$\ny''(x) - 4y(x) = 0.\n$$\n\nUsing direct substitution, it's straightforward to show that $y_1(x) = e^{2x}$ and $y_2(x) = e^{-2x}$ are the solutions to the equation. \n\nLet's keep track of our solutions by putting them into a set $S,$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\left\\{e^{2x}, e^{-2x}\\right\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nComputing the Wronskian of our solutions, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\\\  & =({e}^{2x}){({e}^{-2x})}^{′}-{({e}^{2x})}^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =({e}^{2x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =-2-2 \\\\  & =-4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the Wronskian is not zero, the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent. \n\nBecause the original equation is of degree two, and since the set $S$ contains *precisely* two linearly independent functions, we say that the set $S$ is a fundamental set of solutions to the differential equation.\n\n**Important:** The fundamental set of solutions is not unique. For example, the set $S',$ given by\n\n$$\nS' = \\left\\{4e^{2x}, e^{-2x}\\right\\}\n$$\n\nis also a fundamental set of solutions. \n\nAs a general rule, we tend to pick the simplest set of linearly independent functions when constructing our fundamental set of solutions." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1733749-f7ac-5c62-80aa-f971e91c66d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14498 :tutorial/title "Sets of **linearly independent** on $I$ if the *only* way the linear combination\n\n$$\nk_1 f_1(x) + k_2 f_2(x) + \\cdots + k_n f_n(x)\n$$\n\ncan equal $0$ for all $x \\in I$ is by taking\n\n$$\nk_1 = k_2 = \\cdots = k_n = 0.\n$$\n\nNotice that these definitions closely parallel the notions of linear dependence and independence for vectors in a vector space.\n\nFor example, let's consider the set of functions \n\n$$\n\\{ \\sin x, \\, \\cos x, \\, 2\\sin x \\}\n$$\n\ndefined on $x \\in \\mathbb{R}.$\n\nNotice that for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R},$ we have that\n\n$$\n2 \\cdot \\sin x +\n0 \\cdot \\cos degree $n$ is a set of precisely $n$ linearly independent solutions.\n\nFor example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation \n\n$$\ny''(x) - 4y(x) = 0.\n$$\n\nUsing direct substitution, it's straightforward to show that $y_1(x) = e^{2x}$ and $y_2(x) = e^{-2x}$ are the solutions to the equation. \n\nLet's keep track of our solutions by putting them into a set $S,$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\left\\{e^{2x}, e^{-2x}\\right\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nComputing the Wronskian of our solutions, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\\\  & =({e}^{2x}){({e}^{-2x})}^{′}-{({e}^{2x})}^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =({e}^{2x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =-2-2 \\\\  & =-4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the Wronskian is not zero, the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent. \n\nBecause the original equation is of degree two, and since the set $S$ contains *precisely* two linearly independent functions, we say that the set $S$ is a fundamental set of solutions to the differential equation.\n\n**Important:** The fundamental set of solutions is not unique. For example, the set $S',$ given by\n\n$$\nS' = \\left\\{4e^{2x}, e^{-2x}\\right\\}\n$$\n\nis also a fundamental set of solutions. \n\nAs a general rule, we tend to pick the simplest set of linearly independent functions when constructing our fundamental set of solutions." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1733749-f7ac-5c62-80aa-f971e91c66d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14498 :tutorial/title "Sets of Fundamental Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "d45e0175-eb26-56f3-9d0a-ff5fb71127aa" :step/math-academy-id 593400 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153273}} {:db/id 17592186153329 :tutorial/content "A **fundamental set of solutions** to a homogeneous, linear differential equation of degree $n$ is a set of precisely $n$ linearly independent solutions.\n\nFor example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation \n\n$$\ny''(x) - 4y(x) = 0.\n$$\n\nUsing direct substitution, it's straightforward to show that $y_1(x) = e^{2x}$ and $y_2(x) = e^{-2x}$ are the solutions to the equation. \n\nLet's keep track of our solutions by putting them into a set $S,$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\left\\{e^{2x}, e^{-2x}\\right\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nComputing the Wronskian of our solutions, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\\\  & =({e}^{2x}){({e}^{-2x})}^{′}-{({e}^{2x})}^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =({e}^{2x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x}) \\\\  & =-2-2 \\\\  & =-4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the Wronskian is not zero, the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent. \n\nBecause the original equation is of degree two, and since the set $S$ contains *precisely* two linearly independent functions, we say that the set $S$ is a fundamental set of solutions to the differential equation.\n\n**Important:** The fundamental set of solutions is not unique. "248767b0-4e8f-59a2-a18a-6d7a3f7d1129" :question/math-academy-id "q-334262" :question/problem "$$\n4{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+6x{y}^{′}-2y=0\n$$\n\nConsider the differential equation above. Which of the following statements are true?\n\nI. ${y}_{1}(x)=\\frac{1}{x}$ is a solution to the equation for $x>0.$\n\nII. ${y}_{2}(x)=\\sqrt{x}$ is a solution to the equation for $x>0.$\n\nIII. The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\\infty ).$\n\nSelect all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. \n\nLet's check each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x).$ Notice that $\\frac{1}{x}={x}^{-1},$ so we have:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =-\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =\\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}(\\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+6x(-\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-2(\\frac{1}{x}) & =0 \\\\ (\\frac{8}{x}-\\frac{6}{x}-\\frac{2}{x}) & =0 \\\\ 0 & =0\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.\n\n- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x).$ Notice that $\\sqrt{x}={x}^{\\frac{1}{2}},$ so we have:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\\\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =-\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}(-\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2})+6x(\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2})-2\\sqrt{x} & =0 \\\\ (-{x}^{1/2}+3{x}^{1/2}-2{x}^{1/2}) & =0 \\\\ 0 & =0\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.\n\n- Statement III is true. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1} & {x}^{1/2} \\\\ -{x}^{-2} & \\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={x}^{-1}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}-{x}^{1/2}\\cdot (-{x}^{-2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2}+{x}^{-3/2} \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the  Wronskian is not identically $0$ on $(0,\\infty ),$ the functions are linearly independent. Hence, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\\infty ).$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I, II, and III\"."} :step/id #uuid First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x).$ Notice that $\\frac{1}{x}={x}^{-1},$ so we have:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =-\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =\\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}(\\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+6x(-\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-2(\\frac{1}{x}) & =0 \\\\ (\\frac{8}{x}-\\frac{6}{x}-\\frac{2}{x}) & =0 \\\\ 0 & =0\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.\n\n- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x).$ Notice that $\\sqrt{x}={x}^{\\frac{1}{2}},$ so we have:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\\\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =-\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}(-\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2})+6x(\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2})-2\\sqrt{x} & =0 \\\\ (-{x}^{1/2}+3{x}^{1/2}-2{x}^{1/2}) & =0 \\\\ 0 & =0\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.\n\n- Statement III is true. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\\\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1} & {x}^{1/2} \\\\ -{x}^{-2} & \\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={x}^{-1}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}-{x}^{1/2}\\cdot (-{x}^{-2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2}+{x}^{-3/2} \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the  Wronskian is not identically $0$ on $(0,\\infty ),$ the functions are linearly independent. -4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ -2 & -4\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\\\ 2 & -4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\\\ -10 & 20\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\\,A$):\n\n- For ${\\lambda }_{1}={\\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A-25I & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\\\ -10 & 20\\end{aligned}]-25[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-20 & -10 \\\\ -10 & -5\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector\n\n$$\n{v}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n- For ${\\lambda }_{2}={\\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A-0I & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\\\ -10 & 20\\end{aligned}]-0[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\\\ -10 & 20\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector\n\n$$\n{v}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\\\ 2 & -4\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{5}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{10}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n  \n\nSince the second singular value is ${\\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector\n\n$$\n{u}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nsuch that \n\n$$\n{u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{2}=0\\,\\text{and}\\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.\n$$\n\n \n\nSolving Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$ \n\n$$\n{u}_{2}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}[\\begin{aligned}-2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$\n\n$$\nU=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} & -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}],\\,V=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} & \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048143 the definitions that a $2\\times 2$ matrix $A$ has two repeated singular values $\\sigma_1= \\sigma_2= \\sigma$ if and only if the matrix  $A^TA$ has two repeated eigenvalues $\\lambda_1=\\lambda_2 = \\sigma^2.$  Thus, since $A^TA$ is diagonalizable (because it is symmetric), the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2$ must be two-dimensional. Therefore, \n\n![](images/df/df266614e2576526353248439b7a17431d5e9e43153e1ba225adab3a89321373.svg)\n\nConsequently, we can use any pair of unit orthogonal vectors as a basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2.$ \n\nLet's illustrate this with an example. Consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/ee/ee74c3d4ed7e32388d06b47ed79789d768b54dee61e64d6db57c3eeb582089ae.svg)\n\nLet's find a singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}13 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 13\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since $A^T \\! A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{13}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \\! A$): Since the singular values are equal, we can always take as solutions of $(A^T\\!A-13I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/d1/d1770843817b2557b032743e186dd27106374fef90a2a8e8bb3cfe77b2eb0398.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ -\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c9/c950cf3aff8f9ab47ede762fa9c4451c5e7fc1e78e12fca064ee87d89fcb571e.svg)\n\n**Note:** By swapping the order of eigenvectors in step 3, we swap the vectors $\\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\\mathbf{u}_2$ in step 4. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have\n\n$$\nAB=BC=a\n$$\n\nMoreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore,\n\n$$\nAC = AB\\cdot\\sqrt{2} = a\\sqrt{2}\n$$\n\nFinally, since the perimeter is\n\n$$\np = 26+13\\sqrt{2}\n$$\n\nwe have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\np &= AB + BC + AC \\\\\n26 + 13\\sqrt{2} &= a + a + a\\sqrt{2} \\\\\n26 + 13\\sqrt{2} &= 2a + a\\sqrt{2} \\\\\n13(2 + \\sqrt{2}) &= a(2 + \\sqrt{2}) \\\\\n13(2 + \\sqrt{2}) &= a(2 + \\sqrt{2}) \\\\\n13 &= a\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the length of each leg is $a=13$, and the length of the hypotenuse is\n\n$$\nAC = a \\sqrt{2} = 13 \\sqrt{2}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048921} {:db/id 17592186060221 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186060460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060872 :tutorial/content "In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$, and $90^\\circ$.\n\nConsequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\\boldsymbol{45^\\circ}$-$\\boldsymbol{45^\\circ}$-$\\boldsymbol{90^\\circ}$ triangles**.\n\n![](images/d3/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)\n\nAll $45^\\circ$-$45^\\circ$-$90^\\circ$ triangles share a special property:\n\n> *In any ${45^\\circ}$-${45^\\circ}$-${90^\\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*\n\nTo see why this is, remember that\n\n- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and\n- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.\n\nSo, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h$, then we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nh^{2} &= a^{2} + a^{2} \\\\\nh^{2} &= 2a^{2} \\\\\nh &= \\sqrt{2a^{2}} \\\\\nh &= \\sqrt{2} \\cdot a\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e5fefd4-4ac4-5999-8c6d-0ad927da9ca6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2381 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8b5ee65a-7747-5a0e-9d06-721118b74e10" So, the conjugate of the denominator is\n\n$$\n1\\,{\\color{blue}{-}}\\,\\sqrt{x}\n$$\n\nNow, to rationalize the denominator, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by $1-\\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{1}{1 + \\sqrt{x}} &=  \\\\\n\\frac{1}{1 + \\sqrt{x}} \\cdot \\frac{1 - \\sqrt{x}}{1 - \\sqrt{x}} &=  \\\\\n(1 - \\sqrt{x})/((1 + \\sqrt{x})(1 - \\sqrt{x})) &=  \\\\\n(1 - \\sqrt{x})/(1^{2} - (\\sqrt{x})^{2}) &=  \\\\\n&= \\frac{1 - \\sqrt{x}}{1 - x}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8dde46d5-669e-5c3a-b471-7541b1824862" :tutorial/math-academy-id [{:db/id 17592186069547 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069956 :tutorial/content "The **circumference** of a circle is the length of the path that goes around the is that, for *any* circle, no matter how small or large it is, the ratio of circumference $C$ to diameter $d$ is a fixed number! Specifically,\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{C}{d} = {\\color{blue}\\boldsymbol{\\pi}} \\approx 3.141\\,592\\,654..\n$$\n\nThis important irrational number is called **pi** (pronounced \"pie\") and we use the Greek letter $\\pi$ to express it. So, we can calculate the circumference by using the following formula:\n\n$$\nC = πd\n$$\n\nHere, our circle has diameter $4\\,\\textrm{cm}$, so its circumference is\n\n$$\nC = \\pi \\cdot 4 = 4\\pi \\approx 12.566\\,\\mathrm{cm}\n$$\n\nrounded to three decimal digits.\n\nSince the diameter is twice as long as the radius ($d=2r$), we can also write the formula for the circumference as\n\n$$\nC = \\pi d = 2\\pi r\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e75a0c81-7a99-51d8-85ff-de6951125d7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2423 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3437ac3b-f6ef-5e78-8b46-bca7d485abd4" \\frac{\\text{d}W}{W} & =-\\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\ \\int \\frac{\\text{d}W}{W} & =\\int -\\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\\,\\text{d}x \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =\\operatorname{ln}⁡(\\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+K \\\\ |W| & ={e}^{K}\\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\\\ W & =C\\operatorname{cos}⁡x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $C$ is a constant.\n\nNext, we use the given value "6f396a30-c21c-5a35-935d-80293083bda2" :topic/math-academy-id 6367} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186218195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186218358 :tutorial/content "The Wronskian is a quick way to check whether two solutions of a homogeneous ODE are linearly independent.\n\nIn this lesson, we learn an identity, which tells us how the Wronskian changes with $x$ for an equation of the form \n\n$$\ny''+P(x)y'+Q(x)y=0.\n$$\n\nSuppose $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of the second-order linear homogeneous ODE above on some interval $I.$ Let $W(x)$ be their Wronskian:\n\n$$\n|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & {y}_{2}(x) \\\\ {y}_{1}^{'}(x) & {y}_{2}^{'}(x)\\end{aligned}|\n$$\n\nThen, **Abel's identity** states that the Wronskian satisfies the first-order linear differential equation\n\n$$\nW'(x)=-P(x)W(x).\n$$\n\nSolving this equation via separation of variables gives the general form for $W(x){:}$\n\n$$\nW(x) = C e^{-\\int P(x) \\, \\text{d}x}\n$$\n\nThis allows us to determine the behavior of the Wronskian without knowing the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2.$\n\nFor example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation \n\n$$\ny''+3xy'+e^x y=0\n$$\n\nwith solutions $y_1$ and $y_2,$ and the corresponding Wronskian $W(x).$ Let's determine the differential equation that $W(x)$ must satisfy.\n\nIn our equation, the coefficient of $y'$ is \n\n$$\nP(x)=3x.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into Abel's identity gives \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{W}^{'}(x) & =-3xW(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Watch out!** If the equation is not already in standard form, we should rewrite it before applying Abel’s identity." :tutorial/id #uuid "df1133ef-ff8b-5e3c-bbce-c0f1a484db10" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14746 :tutorial/title 17592186218199}} {:db/id 17592186218199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186218359 :tutorial/content "*Abel's identity* says that if $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of\n\n$$\ny''+p(x)y'+q(x)y=0,\n$$\n\nthen their *Wronskian* $W(x)$ satisfies\n\n$$\nW'(x)=-p(x)W(x).\n$$\n\nTo prove it, we start with the definition\n\n$$\nW(x)=y_1y_2'-y_2y_1'\n$$\n\nand differentiate both sides:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{W}^{'}(x) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{'}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{'}) \\\\  & =\\cancel{{y}_{1}^{'}{y}_{2}^{'}}+{y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{''}-\\cancel{{y}_{2}^{'}{y}_{1}^{'}}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{''} \\\\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{''}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{''}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of $y''+p(x)y'+q(x)y=0$, we have\n\n$$\ny_1''=-p(x)y_1'-q(x)y_1\n\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad\ny_2''=-p(x)y_2'-q(x)y_2.\n$$\n\nNow, we substitute these into the expression for way to check whether two solutions of a homogeneous ODE are linearly independent.\n\nIn this lesson, we learn an identity, which tells us how the Wronskian changes with $x$ for an equation of the form \n\n$$\ny''+P(x)y'+Q(x)y=0.\n$$\n\nSuppose $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of the second-order linear homogeneous ODE above on some interval $I.$ Let $W(x)$ be their Wronskian:\n\n$$\n|\\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & {y}_{2}(x) \\\\ {y}_{1}^{'}(x) & {y}_{2}^{'}(x)\\end{aligned}|\n$$\n\nThen, **Abel's identity** states that the Wronskian satisfies the first-order linear differential equation\n\n$$\nW'(x)=-P(x)W(x).\n$$\n\nSolving this equation via separation of variables gives the general form for $W(x){:}$\n\n$$\nW(x) = C e^{-\\int P(x) \\, \\text{d}x}\n$$\n\nThis allows us to determine the behavior of the Wronskian without knowing the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2.$\n\nFor example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation \n\n$$\ny''+3xy'+e^x y=0\n$$\n\nwith solutions $y_1$ and $y_2,$ and the corresponding Wronskian $W(x).$ Let's determine the differential equation that $W(x)$ must satisfy.\n\nIn our equation, the coefficient of $y'$ is \n\n$$\nP(x)=3x.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into Abel's identity gives \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{W}^{'}(x) & =-3xW(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Watch out!** If the equation is not already in standard form, we should rewrite it before applying Abel’s identity." :tutorial/id #uuid "df1133ef-ff8b-5e3c-bbce-c0f1a484db10" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14746 :tutorial/title "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region\n$D=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 2,\\,\\,1\\le y\\le 3\\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the origin is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{4}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}\\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}\\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{[\\frac{4}{3}y+\\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\\frac{4}{3}+\\frac{1}{3})) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}(13-\\frac{5}{3}) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}\\cdot \\frac{34}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{17M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{0}^{2}=\\frac{17}{3}\\,⇒\\,{R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{17}{3}}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186198665 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region\n$D=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 1,\\,\\,4\\le y\\le 6\\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{2}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{4}^{6}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{4}^{6}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{4}^{6}\\frac{1}{3}(1-0)\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{6}{\\int }_{4}^{6}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{6}[y]_{4}^{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{6}(6-4) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{y}^{2}=\\frac{1}{3}\\,⇒\\,{R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{3}}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186235554 :question/id #uuid mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{2}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{\\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}(\\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\\cdot 3=9.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{9}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}{\\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}(\\frac{64}{3}-\\frac{1}{3})\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}21\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}{\\int }_{2}^{5}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}[y]_{2}^{5} \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}(5-2) \\\\  & =7M.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{y}^{2}=7\\,⇒\\,{R}_{y}=\\sqrt{7}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186198419 Its mass density at any point is given by $\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nIn polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by\n\n$$\nD=\\{(r,\\theta )\\,:\\,1\\le r\\le 2,\\,\\,0\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{\\pi }{2}\\}.\n$$\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (r,\\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta ,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (r,\\theta )$ is the mass density function.\n\nAlso, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\\lambda (r,\\theta )=\\frac{3}{7}Mr\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .$\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (r,\\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}{\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M({\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\\,\\text{d}r)({\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot \\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\\cdot {[-\\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\\pi /2} \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot (\\frac{32}{5}-\\frac{1}{5})\\cdot (-0+\\frac{1}{3}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot \\frac{31}{5}\\cdot \\frac{1}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{31M}{35}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{31M}{35}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{31}{35}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186198957 :question/id #uuid "b6fbab0f-40fd-5c65-87d5-1b56f0245d59" Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{3}{4}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation\n\n$$\nD=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 2,\\,\\,0\\le y\\le x\\}.\n$$\n\nHence, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{2}\\cdot \\frac{3}{4}My\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{3M}{4}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{3M}{4}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{[\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{3M}{4}{\\int }_{0}^{2}\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{3M}{4}{[\\frac{1}{10}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{3M}{4}\\cdot \\frac{16}{5} \\\\  & =\\frac{12M}{5}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{12M}{5}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{12}{5}} \\\\  & =2\\sqrt{\\frac{3}{5}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186198956 :question/id #uuid "2db88b84-fe57-56b2-8d78-b4ac01dd1164" point on the plate is given by $\\lambda (x,y)=15My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the origin is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation\n\n$$\nD={(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 1,\\,\\,{x}^{2}\\le y\\le x}.\n$$\n\nHence, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\cdot 15My\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =15M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =15M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{[\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=x}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =15M{\\int }_{0}^{1}(\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}+\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})-(\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6}+\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{8})\\text{d}x \\\\  & =15M{\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{3}{4}{x}^{4}-\\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6}-\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{8}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =15M{[\\frac{3}{20}{x}^{5}-\\frac{1}{14}{x}^{7}-\\frac{1}{36}{x}^{9}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =15M(\\frac{3}{20}-\\frac{1}{14}-\\frac{1}{36}) \\\\  & =15M\\cdot \\frac{16}{315} \\\\  & =\\frac{16M}{21}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{16M}{21}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{16}{21}} \\\\  & =\\frac{\\sqrt{16}}{\\sqrt{21}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4}{\\sqrt{21}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4\\sqrt{21}}{21}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186369936 :question/id #uuid "fd312e64-46c6-5ed4-b65d-22fbf05ffa3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-163611" }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{[\\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\\sqrt{x}}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int applies to rotating bodies.\n\nRecall that the *center of mass* of a plane lamina is defined as the point $(\\bar{x},\\bar{y})$ in the coordinate plane where the entire mass of the lamina could be concentrated to produce the same *total moment* about the coordinate axes as the original laminar. \n\nAnalogously, the **radius of gyration** of a plane lamina is the distance $R$ from an axis of rotation $L$ that the entire mass $M$ of the lamina would need to be concentrated to produce the same *moment of inertia* as the original lamina. \n\n![](images/c9/c9999bf30a93a857db731488739f0a640edc7b91de907cd772b777489a011fb8.png)\n\nTo derive an explicit formula for the radius of gyration, recall that the moment of inertia of a particle $P$ of mass $m$ at a distance of $r$ from an axis of rotation equals\n\n$$\nmr^2.\n$$\n\nSo, for a particle of mass $M$ at a distance of $R$ from the axis of rotation $L,$ the moment of inertia about $L$ is given by\n\n$$\nMR^2.\n$$\n\nThe radius of gyration is defined as the distance $R$ that a particle of mass $M$ must be placed to give the same moment of inertia as the original lamina. Therefore, it is the solution to the equation\n\n$$\nI = MR^2,\n$$\n\nwhere $I$ is the moment of inertia of the lamina about $L.$\n\nRearranging this equation, we find that the radius of gyration is given by\n\n$$\nR = \\sqrt{\\dfrac{I}{M}}.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9694de04-ca38-5d55-a60f-6663ca34e7cf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5074 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid #uuid "c52b9e07-a1a1-59e3-9b59-f3ce7c050afb" :question/math-academy-id "q-163578" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region\n$D=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 1,\\,\\,0\\le y\\le 3\\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the origin is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\\cdot 3=3.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{3}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}{\\int }_{0}^{3}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}{\\int =\\frac{M}{3}{[\\frac{1}{3}y+\\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}(1+9) \\\\  & of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\\cdot 3=9.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{9}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}{\\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}(\\frac{64}{3}-\\frac{1}{3})\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{9}{\\int }_{2}^{5}21\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}{\\int }_{2}^{5}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}[y]_{2}^{5} \\\\  & =\\frac{7M}{3}(5-2) \\\\  & =7M.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{y}^{2}=7\\,⇒\\,{R}_{y}=\\sqrt{7}.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the origin is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{4}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{4}{\\int }_{1}^{3}\\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}\\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{[\\frac{4}{3}y+\\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\\frac{4}{3}+\\frac{1}{3})) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}(13-\\frac{5}{3}) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}\\cdot \\frac{34}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{17M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{0}^{2}=\\frac{17}{3}\\,⇒\\,{R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{17}{3}}.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "147cc4dc-7dc1-5126-916a-8cec1032d28e" :step/next {:db/id region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nIn polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by\n\n$$\nD=\\{(r,\\theta )\\,:\\,1\\le r\\le 2,\\,\\,0\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{\\pi }{2}\\}.\n$$\n\nThe moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (r,\\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta ,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (r,\\theta )$ is the mass density function.\n\nAlso, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\\lambda (r,\\theta )=\\frac{3}{7}Mr\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .$\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (r,\\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M{\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}{\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}r\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M({\\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\\,\\text{d}r)({\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\,\\text{d}\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot \\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\\cdot {[-\\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\\pi /2} \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot (\\frac{32}{5}-\\frac{1}{5})\\cdot (-0+\\frac{1}{3}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{7}M\\cdot \\frac{31}{5}\\cdot \\frac{1}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{31M}{35}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{31M}{35}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{31}{35}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "5a28356f-4b44-5c8b-b9c7-4d02b2d94106"} {:db/id 17592186479155 :step/content The region $D$ is a type I region with representation\n\n$$\nD=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 1,\\,\\,0\\le y\\le \\sqrt{x}\\}.\n$$\n\nHence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\\cdot 4My\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{[\\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\\sqrt{x}}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =M{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{M}{3}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{3}} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "6aa4a18d-6a7f-5ff6-bc60-411ff63cf5eb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479150}} {:db/id 17592186479156 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281676 The region $D$ is a type I region with representation\n\n$$\nD=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,0\\le x\\le 1,\\,\\,0\\le y\\le \\sqrt{x}\\}.\n$$\n\nHence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\\cdot 4My\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{[\\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\\sqrt{x}}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =4M{\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =M{\\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =M{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{M}{3}\\cdot \\frac{1}{M}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{\\frac{1}{3}} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "6aa4a18d-6a7f-5ff6-bc60-411ff63cf5eb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479150}} {:db/id 17592186479150 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198651 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "de217583-4705-57c2-81c7-b02676db7154" :question/math-academy-id "q-163582" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region\n$D=\\{(x,y)\\,:\\,1\\le x\\le 2,\\,\\,1\\le y\\le 3\\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by\n${R}_{x}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by\n${R}_{y}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.\n\n- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by\n${R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$\nwhere ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.\n\nThe moment of inertia about the origin is defined as\n\n$$\n{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.\n\nThe area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by\n\n$$\n\\lambda (x,y)=\\frac{M}{A}=\\frac{M}{2}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{\\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}{[\\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}(\\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{\\int }_{1}^{3}\\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}{[\\frac{7}{3}y+\\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\\frac{7}{3}-\\frac{1}{3}) \\\\  & =\\frac{M}{2}\\cdot \\frac{40}{3} \\\\  & =\\frac{20M}{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,\n\n$$\n{R}_{0}^{2}=\\frac{20}{3}\\,⇒\\,{R}_{0}=\\sqrt{\\frac{20}{3}}=2\\sqrt{\\frac{5}{3}}.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 653404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167584}} {:db/id 17592186167584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168065 :tutorial/content "Suppose we fix a basis $\\mathcal{B}=\\{ \\mathbf{b}_1, \\mathbf{b}_2, \\ldots, \\mathbf{b}_n \\}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\\mathbb{R}$ (note that \"finite-dimensional\" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\\mathbf{v} \\in V$ using the coordinates of $\\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\\mathcal{B} \\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c9/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)\n\nThis defines a bijective mapping $\\phi: V\\to \\mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:\n\n- $\\phi(\\mathbf{u}+\\mathbf{v}) = \\phi(\\mathbf{u}) + \\phi(\\mathbf{v})$ for any $\\mathbf{u}, \\mathbf{v} \\in V,$ and\n\n- $\\phi(\\alpha \\mathbf{v}) = \\alpha \\phi(\\mathbf{v})$ for any $\\mathbf{v} \\in V$ and any $\\alpha \\in \\mathbb{R}.$\n\nBecause of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.\n\nSo, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\\geq 1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e501b24f-7ea0-5110-a4c5-e8739ea9ac11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4964 :step/math-academy-id 653404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167584}} {:db/id 17592186167584 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168065 :tutorial/content "Suppose we fix a basis $\\mathcal{B}=\\{ \\mathbf{b}_1, \\mathbf{b}_2, \\ldots, \\mathbf{b}_n \\}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\\mathbb{R}$ (note that \"finite-dimensional\" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\\mathbf{v} \\in V$ using the coordinates of $\\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\\mathcal{B} \\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c9/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)\n\nThis defines a bijective mapping $\\phi: V\\to \\mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:\n\n- $\\phi(\\mathbf{u}+\\mathbf{v}) = \\phi(\\mathbf{u}) + \\phi(\\mathbf{v})$ for any $\\mathbf{u}, \\mathbf{v} \\in V,$ and\n\n- $\\phi(\\alpha \\mathbf{v}) = \\alpha \\phi(\\mathbf{v})$ for any $\\mathbf{v} \\in V$ and any $\\alpha \\in \\mathbb{R}.$\n\nBecause of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.\n\nSo, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\\geq 1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e501b24f-7ea0-5110-a4c5-e8739ea9ac11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4964 :tutorial/title "Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces"} :step/id #uuid "f13dd7dd-f256-5871-9c5b-37fcd35b85a3" :step/math-academy-id 653407} {:db/id 17592186168065 :tutorial/content "Suppose we fix a basis $\\mathcal{B}=\\{ \\mathbf{b}_1, \\mathbf{b}_2, \\ldots, \\mathbf{b}_n \\}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\\mathbb{R}$ (note that \"finite-dimensional\" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ \n\nSo, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\\,j \\\\  & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\\,i+\\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\\,j \\\\  & =2x\\,i-6y\\,j \\\\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\\,i-6(1)\\,j \\\\  & =6\\,i-6\\,j \\\\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$\n\nFinally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\\\ \\frac{x-3}{6} & =\\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\\\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\\\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\\\ -x+3 & =y-1 $P(1,-1).$\n\n- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\\nabla f = \\langle 2x, 2y \\rangle.$ Therefore, $$\\nabla f(1,-1) = \\langle 2, -2 \\rangle.$$\n- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\\langle 1,1 \\rangle$ is parallel to the level curve.\n- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain $$\\nabla f(1,-1)\\cdot \\langle 1,1 \\rangle = \\langle 2, -2\\rangle \\cdot \\langle 1,1 \\rangle = 0.$$\n\nThis means that particular nature reserve. The population of wolves $W(t)$ after $t$ decades of observations is given by\n\n$W(t) = W_{0} \\cdot 4^{t}$,\n\nwhere $W_{0}$ represents the wolves' population at the beginning of the study. If there were $3\\,200$ wolves after $3$ decades, how many wolves were there at the beginning of the study?" :question/worked-solution "There are $3\\,200$ wolves $3$ decades after the scientists started studying the wolf population, so\n\n$$\nW(3) = 3\\,200\n$$\n\nTo find the initial number of wolves $W_0$, we substitute $t=3$ and\n\n$$\nW(3) = 3\\,200\n$$\n\ninto the given equation and solve for $W_0$, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nW(3) &= W_{0} \\cdot 4^{3} \\\\\n3200 &= W_{0} \\cdot 64 \\\\\nW_{0} &= \\frac{3200}{64} \\\\\nW_{0} &= 50\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, there were $50$ wolves at the beginning of the study."} {:db/id 17592186147747 :question/id #uuid "6cdcb31d-ea78-57af-a538-ae6af6444b73" :question/math-academy-id "q-212627"} {:db/id 17592186147754 :question/id #uuid "a35ecb46-c963-5327-9e18-393d06a9f0b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-25575"} {:db/id 17592186049158} {:db/id 17592186049643} {:db/id 17592186049980} {:db/id 17592186050870} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186148270} :activity/id #uuid "66824b85-374f-5412-9f2f-47a7d45ad385" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048995 :topic/id #uuid "d1edd866-fc11-5971-b454-c205e7356f7f" :topic/math-academy-id 2464} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186148270 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148795 :tutorial/content "We can use our knowledge of solving exponential equations to obtain information about a system that follows an exponential growth model.\n\nFor example, suppose that the revenue $R(t)$, in millions of dollars, of a rapidly growing startup company is given by the function\n\n$$\nR(t) = 2\\cdot 3^t\n$$\n\nwhere $t$ is the number of years since the company was incorporated. How long will it take for the company's revenue to reach $\\[math]18$ million?\n\nTo find the solution to this problem, we need to solve the equation $R(t) = 18$. This gives us the equation\n\n$$\n2\\cdot 3^t = 18\n$$\n\nTo solve this equation, we first divide both sides by $2{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n2 \\cdot 3^{t} &= 18 \\\\\n\\frac{2 \\cdot 3^{t}}{2} &= \\frac{18}{2} \\\\\n\\frac{2 \\cdot 3^{t}}{2} &= 9 \\\\\n3^{t} &= 9\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we notice that $9$ is a power of $3$, because $9=3^2$. So we get\n\n$$\n3^{\\color{blue}t} = 3^{\\color{blue}2}\n$$\n\nThe bases of both exponents are equal, so the powers must also be equal. Therefore, our solution is\n\n$$\nt = {\\color{blue}2}\n$$\n\nWe conclude that it will take the company $\\color{blue}2$ years to reach a revenue of $\\[/math]18$ million." :tutorial/id #uuid $N_0$ is a constant. If there are $5\\,000$ users $5$ weeks after launch, can we determine how many users the app had when it launched?\n\nHere, $N_0$ represents the initial number of users, and this is what we're trying to find.\n\nFrom the given information, we know that\n\n$$\nN(5) = 5\\,000\n$$\n\nSo let's plug this into our function:\n\n$$\n5\\,000 = N_0(1.2)^5\n$$\n\nTo solve this equation, we can divide both sides by $(1.2)^5{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n(5000)/((1.2)^{5}) &= (N_{0}(1.2)^{5})/((1.2)^{5}) \\\\\n(5000)/((1.2)^{5}) &= (N_{0}(1.2)^{5})/((1.2)^{5}) \\\\\n(5000)/((1.2)^{5}) &= N_{0}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's flip the equation around to make it easier to work with.\n\n$$\nN_0 = \\dfrac{5\\,000}{(1.2)^5}\n$$\n\nWe can now work out $N_0$ using a calculator. We find that\n\n$$\nN_0\\approx 2\\,009\n$$\n\nWe have rounded to the nearest integer since $N_0$ refers to a number of people.\n\nTherefore, when it launched, the app had $2\\,009$ users." :tutorial/id #uuid "ae3d753f-4a2d-55b0-9fb7-a3f746f66018" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8854 :tutorial/title "Unknown Initial Values"} :step/id #uuid "da8a83fe-da24-58c8-be84-aad5b70f01a0" :step/math-academy-id 196875 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148275}} {:db/id 17592186148275 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147424 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147179 :question/id #uuid "07a30fba-ad4b-56a0-b6ce-21941d106b38" :question/math-academy-id "e-14276"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2c127787-8a31-524b-8b7d-68c15b714335" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147747} {:db/id 17592186147754}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving for an Unknown Initial Value"} :step/id #uuid "20edaa81-4eeb-5d4b-98a7-837cb86e910d" :step/math-academy-id 196876}] :activity/title "Solving Exponential Growth Problems" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186147664} {:db/id 17592186148270 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148795 :tutorial/content "We can use our knowledge of solving exponential equations to obtain information about a system that follows an exponential growth model.\n\nFor example, suppose that the revenue $R(t)$, in millions of dollars, of a rapidly growing startup company is given by the function\n\n$$\nR(t) = 2\\cdot 3^t\n$$\n\nwhere $t$ is the number of years since the company was incorporated. ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2xy=0 \\\\ -6y+3xy=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFactoring the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\\\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.\n\n- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4x(1-0.25x)-2x(0) & =0 \\\\ 4x(0.25x-1) & =0 \\\\ x & =0,\\,4.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(4,0).$\n\n- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4(2)(1-0.25(2))-2(2)y & =0 \\\\ 4-4y & =0 \\\\ y & =1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus, another equilibrium is $(2,1).$\n\nTherefore, the equilibria of the model are\n\n$$\n(0,0),\\,(4,0),\\,(2,1).\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186480667 :question/id #uuid "6f820e7d-e65e-5149-80bc-fca1cd9160a9" :question/math-academy-id 3231} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167876 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168015 :tutorial/content "The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, \n\n- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and\n\n- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.\n\nThe only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then \n\n$$\nx' = ax(1-hx).\n$$\n\nRecall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\\,⇒\\,x=0,\\,\\frac{1}{h}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the equilibria are $x=0$ and
