:step/content {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nhas equilibria at\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1 - \\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).\n$$\n\nNotice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when \n\n$$\nh < \\dfrac{d}{c},\n$$\n\nwhich guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.\n\nWe now evaluate the Jacobian matrix\n![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)\nat the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get\n\n![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)\n\nBecause we are considering the case when $h < \\dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{c}{h}\\left(\\dfrac{d}{c}-h\\right) > 0.\n$$\n\nThe eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\\lambda_2 = \\dfrac{c}{h}\\left(\\dfrac{d}{c}-h\\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.\n\nAnalyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.\n\nA typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \\dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.\n\n![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)\n\nThe global picture is the following:\n\n- There are two straight-line types of solutions:\n\n- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h},0\\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.\n\n- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.\n\n- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1 - \\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).$\n\nThe corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.\n\n![](images/a7/a7673170825344e1831f2ba01ce4c20f10091380ff4e116f3b6bd9e7666e51aa.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ce000cd-7913-5e8e-90d2-3a5a820db4f4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14543 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b61ca7e0-a217-5555-8d14-3f0d56453cb5" :step/math-academy-id 590167 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167885}} {:db/id 17592186167880 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166928 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166559 :question/id #uuid "3e280ec5-c95a-5ca6-ba2e-edc4cf653ea3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21736"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4936474f-5e5f-5da2-8242-1b48336a836c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048881}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167252} {:db/id 17592186167261} {:db/id 17592186370423} {:db/id 17592186370540} {:db/id 17592186480691}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case"} :step/id #uuid "33bb23bb-bd23-5d38-9487-0ff5ffdddc57" :step/math-academy-id 590168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167881}} {:db/id 17592186167881 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168017 :tutorial/content "Again, recall that the system\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nhas equilibria at\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1 - \\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).\n$$\n\nWe have already considered the case when $h < \\dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.\n\n- When $h = \\dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right) = \\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, 0\\right)\n$$\n\n- When $h > \\dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium is in the fourth quadrant (its $y$-coordinate is negative). So, we have only two equilibria that make sense in the context of the model:\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right)\n$$\n\nHence, we get only two equilibria. \n\nThe trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at\n\n$$\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right)\n$$\n\nwill be an *asymptotically stable sink*.\n\nA typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \\geq \\dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.\n\n![](images/b9/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)\n\nThe global picture is the following:\n\n- There are two straight-line types of solutions:\n\n- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h},0\\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.\n\n- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.\n\n- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\\right).$\n\nThe corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.\n\n![](images/cd/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)\n\nEventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.\n\nLet's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "92ed0e52-b2f2-5d81-99c3-60526aa8f13a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14547 :tutorial/title "Predator "51d64692-6d2f-5189-bd9c-6590b8925293" :step/math-academy-id 590173} {:db/id 17592186167883 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168028 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\\mathbf{x}'(t) = \\mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nthe equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\\\ -cy+dxy=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFactoring the second equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\\\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, $y=0$ or $x=\\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.\n\n- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\\\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\\\ x & =0,\\,\\frac{1}{h}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h},0\\right).$\n\n- If $x=\\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}a(\\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\\frac{c}{d}))-b(\\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\\\ a(1-\\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\\\ a(1-\\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\\\ y & =\\frac{a}{b}(1-\\frac{c}{d}h).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus, another equilibrium is $\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1-\\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).$\n\nTherefore, the equilibria of the model are\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h},0\\right), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1-\\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79e78f76-a29e-544f-a86b-9f714e69cf63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14597 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.\n\nTo classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.\n\nLet's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$\n\nNow, we compute the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\\,-\\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\\,-\\,2hx)-by, & \\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\\,-\\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\\\ \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus, the Jacobian matrix is\n![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)\n\nNext, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get\n\n![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)\n\nThe eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.\n\nThus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :tutorial/id #uuid "feef6e7a-79a2-5b71-8cec-dc45e305ec52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14598 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\\\ ![](images/30/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get\n\n![](images/fc/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)\n\nThe eigenvalues of ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get\n\n![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)\n\nThe eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.\n\nThus, the equilibrium at the origin system $\\mathbf{x}'(t) = \\mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\\\ \\dfrac{a}{b}\\left(1-\\dfrac{c}{d}h\\right)\\right).$\n\nTherefore, the equilibria of the model are\n\n$$\n(0,0), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{1}{h},0\\right), \\qquad\n\\left(\\dfrac{c}{d}, }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWe wish to compute ${I}^{′}(t),$ where\n\n$$\nI(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nDifferentiating under the integral sign, we get\n\n$$\n{I}^{′}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{∂}{∂t}[(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}]\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nNext, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂t}[(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}] & =2(2x+{e}^{t})\\cdot \\frac{∂}{∂t}(2x+{e}^{t}) \\\\  & =2(2x+{e}^{t})\\cdot {e}^{t} \\\\  & =2{e}^{t}(2x+{e}^{t})\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting this back into our integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{t}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =2{e}^{t}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}2x\\,\\text{d}x+{\\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1}+{e}^{t}\\cdot x{|}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =1+{e}^{t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n{I}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{t}(1+{e}^{t}).\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186308705 :question/id #uuid "932e788a-5d6d-5848-ade5-e4094868063b" :question/math-academy-id If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\\times [c,d]$ and $\\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function\n\n$$\nF(t)={\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x\n$$\n\nis differentiable on $(c,d),$ and\n\n$$\n{F}^{′}(t)=\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x={\\int }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each function:\n\n- For the first function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{1}(x,t)=\\sqrt{x+t}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{x+t}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R$ (since $x+t\\ge c>0$ on $R$). Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>0.$\n\n- For the second function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{2}(x,t)=\\frac{xt}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\\frac{x({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})-2x{t}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>0.$\n\n- For the third function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{3}(x,t)=\\frac{1}{x-t}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>1$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that for $t>1$ and $x\\in [0,1],$ the denominator $x-t$ never vanishes on $R,$ so ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>1.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I, II, and III.\""} {:db/id 17592186311551 :question/id #uuid "57d1f543-d099-580f-9280-d60da64177c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-335248" Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\\frac{x}{(x-t)^{2}}\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t<0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"II and III only.\""} {:db/id 17592186049877} x\n=\n\\int_{a}^b \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial t}(x,t)\\,\\textrm{d} x.\n$$\n\nWe wish to compute $I'(t),$ where\n\n$$\nI(t)=\\int_{-1}^{1} (3x-t^2)^2\\,\\textrm{d}x.\n$$\n\nDifferentiating under =-4t(3x-{t}^{2}).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting this back into our integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}-4t(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =-4t{\\int }_{-1}^{1}(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{-1}^{1}(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}3x\\,\\text{d}x-{\\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{1}-{t}^{2}x{|}_{-1}^{1} \\\\  & =0-2{t}^{2} \\\\  & =-2{t}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & =-4t(-2{t}^{2}) \\\\  & =8{t}^{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5875ac89-b808-53fa-b46e-33fadfb23647" }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWe wish to compute ${I}^{′}(t),$ where\n\n$$\nI(t)={\\int }_{0}^{2}(x-4{t}^{3})^{2}\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nDifferentiating under the integral sign, we get\n\n$$\n{I}^{′}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{2}\\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x-4{t}^{3})^{2}]\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nNext, let's \\\\  & =-24{t}^{2}(x-4{t}^{3})\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting this back into our integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}-24{t}^{2}(x-4{t}^{3})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =-24{t}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{2}(x-4{t}^{3})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{0}^{2}(x-4{t}^{3})\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}x\\,\\text{d}x-{\\int }_{0}^{2}4{t}^{3}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{2}-4{t}^{3}x{|}_{0}^{2} \\\\  & =2-8{t}^{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & =-24{t}^{2}(2-8{t}^{3}) \\\\  & =48{t}^{2}(4{t}^{3}-1).\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-{t}^{2}x}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t\\in R$\n- **II.** ${F}_{2}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t\\ge 0$\n- **III.** ${F}_{3}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t>0$\n\nSelect all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\\times [c,d]$ and $\\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function\n\n$$\nF(t)={\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x\n$$\n\nis differentiable on $(c,d),$ and\n\n$$\n{F}^{′}(t)=\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x={\\int }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each function:\n\n- For the first function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{1}(x,t)={e}^{-{t}^{2}x}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}\\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=-2tx{e}^{-{t}^{2}x},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$\n\n- For the second function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{2}(x,t)=|x-t|.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}\\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆[0,1],$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ However, the partial derivative\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}={\\begin{aligned}-1,\\,x>t \\\\ 1,\\,x<t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\ndoes *not* exist whenever $x=t={t}_{0},$ and is therefore not defined everywhere on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.\n\n- For the third function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{3}(x,t)=\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\\frac{2t}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t>0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III only.\""} :step/id #uuid }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWe wish to compute ${I}^{′}(t),$ where\n\n$$\nI(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nDifferentiating under the integral sign, we get\n\n$$\n{I}^{′}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{∂}{∂t}[(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}]\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nNext, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂t}[(2x+{e}^{t})^{2}] & =2(2x+{e}^{t})\\cdot \\frac{∂}{∂t}(2x+{e}^{t}) \\\\  & =2(2x+{e}^{t})\\cdot {e}^{t} \\\\  & =2{e}^{t}(2x+{e}^{t})\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting this back into our integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{t}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =2{e}^{t}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+{e}^{t})\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}2x\\,\\text{d}x+{\\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1}+{e}^{t}\\cdot x{|}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =1+{e}^{t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n{I}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{t}(1+{e}^{t}).\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "e52f37a8-a447-5f85-8c13-490937937ec2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495246}} {:db/id 17592186495226 Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\\frac{2t}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t>0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III only.\""} :step/id #uuid That is, for any $(x,y)$ pair, we have\n\n$$\nk = \\dfrac{y}{x}\n$$\n\nwhere $k$ is a fixed number called the **constant of proportionality** or **constant of variation.**\n\nAs a concrete example, let's consider the table below.\n\n| $x$ | $y$ |\n| --- | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ |\n| $2$ | $4$ |\n| $4$ | $8$ |\n\nDo $x$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship?\n\nTo determine whether $x$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship, we first add a new\n\n$$\n\\dfrac yx\n$$\n\ncolumn:\n\n| $x$ | $y$ | $\\dfrac{y}{x}$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ |  |\n| $2$ | $4$ |  |\n| $4$ | $8$ |  |\n\nNext, we compute\n\n$$\n\\dfrac yx\n$$\n\nfor each row:\n\n| $x$ | $y$ | $\\dfrac{y}{x}$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ | $2\\div 1 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n| $2$ | $4$ | $4\\div 2 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n| $4$ | $8$ | $8\\div 4 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n\nSince all the entries in the third column have the same value, this table does indeed represent a proportional relationship. In this case, the constant of proportionality\n\n$$\nk = {\\color{blue}{2}}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "935405f7-2fd3-5fb6-a9ef-e3d74aa721b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8207 :tutorial/title That is, for any $(x,y)$ pair, we have\n\n$$\nk = \\dfrac{y}{x}\n$$\n\nwhere $k$ is a fixed number called the **constant of proportionality** or **constant of variation.**\n\nAs a concrete example, let's consider the table below.\n\n| $x$ | $y$ |\n| --- | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ |\n| $2$ | $4$ |\n| $4$ | $8$ |\n\nDo $x$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship?\n\nTo determine whether $x$ and $y$ have a proportional relationship, we first add a new\n\n$$\n\\dfrac yx\n$$\n\ncolumn:\n\n| $x$ | $y$ | $\\dfrac{y}{x}$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ |  |\n| $2$ | $4$ |  |\n| $4$ | $8$ |  |\n\nNext, we compute\n\n$$\n\\dfrac yx\n$$\n\nfor each row:\n\n| $x$ | $y$ | $\\dfrac{y}{x}$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| $1$ | $2$ | $2\\div 1 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n| $2$ | $4$ | $4\\div 2 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n| $4$ | $8$ | $8\\div 4 = {\\color{blue}{2}}$ |\n\nSince all the entries in the third column have the same value, this table does indeed represent a proportional relationship. the formula for the line integral is given by\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{C}f(x,y)\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta \\,.\n$$\n\n \n\nThe connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\cdot \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta , \\\\ y & =r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, along our curve, we have $x=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta $, where $0\\le \\theta \\le \\pi .$\n\nNow, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & ={(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )}^{2} \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand therefore\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  & =\\sqrt{{(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )}^{2}+{(2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta }_{2}}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta \\,.\n$$\n\n \n\nThe connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta =2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta , \\\\ y & =r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, along our curve, we have $x=2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta $ and $y=2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta $, where $0\\le \\theta \\le \\frac{\\pi }{4}.$  \n\nNow, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) & =(2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}-(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )^{2} \\\\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =4\\operatorname{cos}⁡2\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(2)=0,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand therefore\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  & =\\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{4} \\\\  & =2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\\,\\text{d}s & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /4}f(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )\\,\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /4}4\\operatorname{cos}⁡2\\theta \\cdot 2\\cdot \\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi /4}8\\operatorname{cos}⁡2\\theta \\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & =4\\operatorname{sin}⁡2\\theta \\,{|}_{0}^{\\pi /4} \\\\  & =4(\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\pi /2)-\\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\\\  & =4\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "76874250-4cf6-5cac-b8f3-c61d135f6019" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483435}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid and ${\\sigma }_{2}=0.$\nAlso, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$\n\nTherefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{2} & 0 \\\\ \\sqrt{2} & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ The algorithm for computing an SVD of a rectangular $m\\times n$ matrix $(m\\neq n)$ is similar to the algorithm for square matrices.\n\nAs an example, let's consider the matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/f6/f65e0eee905da85ce0be4bbf39546c2b31c2bac082ff00a6a1d54fd5b89a4a4e.svg)\n\nNotice that $A$ is a ${\\color{blue}{3}}\\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix. So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write\n\n$$\nA=U \\Sigma V^T,\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\Sigma$ is a ${\\color{blue}{3}}\\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{blue}{3}} \\times {\\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{red}{2}} \\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.\n\nWe proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\lambda_1 = 4, \\qquad \\lambda_2 = 2.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_1} =  2,  \\qquad \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_2} =  \\sqrt{2}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T \\! A - \\lambda_1 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ and $(A^T \\! A - \\lambda_2 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The matrix $U$ is a $3\\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) \nsuch that \n![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)\nSolving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c2/c2bbd771d886da6b3a369b7e03345d1be75c18c26c66590598581d2d99590524.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "670f2f0c-5dc5-54ae-9a39-2166ee2414fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4893 to find an SVD for the $2\\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)\n\nDirectly applying the standard approach to $A$ could \\left(U \\Sigma V^T\\right)^T=V\\Sigma^T U^T\n$$\n\nis an SVD for $A.$  \n\nGoing through our usual process, we find that an SVD for $A^T$ is\n\n![](images/78/7802bcf50374a71efc4c0a7754c5628e88e7f1dfac345bc9e590cfcebd89d8d1.svg)\n\nTaking the transpose of the above equation. we find that an SVD for $A$ :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.\n\nThis happens, for example, when:\n\n- an eigenvalue is repeated, or\n\n- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.\n\nIn these cases, we proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  \n\nFor example, we solve an equation of the form\n\n$$\n(A^T A - \\lambda I)\\mathbf{v} = \\mathbf{0},\n$$\n\nor, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0, \\qquad \\mathbf{u}_2 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0.\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  \n\nThis shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{v} = x\\,\\mathbf{b}_1 + y\\,\\mathbf{b}_2,\n$$\n\nwhere $x$ and $y$ are free variables.\n\n- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  \n\nWe usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.\n\n- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  \n\nIf the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.\n\n- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  \n\nAfter that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.\n\nThese unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$\n\n**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:\n\n- belong to the correct solution space,\n\n- are mutually orthogonal, and\n\n- have norm $1.$\n\nLet's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162227} {:db/id 17592186162858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write\n\n$$\nA=U \\Sigma V^T,\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\Sigma$ is a ${\\color{blue}{3}}\\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{blue}{3}} \\times {\\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{red}{2}} \\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.\n\nWe proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\lambda_1 = 4, \\qquad \\lambda_2 = 2.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_1} =  2,  \\qquad \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_2} =  \\sqrt{2}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). A - \\lambda_2 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The matrix $U$ is a $3\\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. 648301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162948}} {:db/id 17592186385970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.\n\nThis happens, for example, when:\n\n- an eigenvalue is repeated, or\n\n- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.\n\nIn these cases, we proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  \n\nFor example, we solve an equation of the form\n\n$$\n(A^T A - \\lambda I)\\mathbf{v} = \\mathbf{0},\n$$\n\nor, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0, \\qquad \\mathbf{u}_2 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0.\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  \n\nThis shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{v} = x\\,\\mathbf{b}_1 + y\\,\\mathbf{b}_2,\n$$\n\nwhere $x$ and $y$ are free variables.\n\n- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  \n\nWe usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.\n\n- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  \n\nIf the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.\n\n- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  \n\nAfter that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.\n\nThese unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$\n\n**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:\n\n- belong to the correct solution space,\n\n- are mutually orthogonal, and\n\n- have norm $1.$\n\nLet's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}} {:db/id 17592186162948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163258 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)\n\nDirectly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\\times 4$ matrix $A^T \\! [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.\nThe course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.\nThe course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.\nStudents next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.\nApplications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.\nThe course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.\nLaplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.\nThe course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid global errors: a method may be accurate in a single step, but if it is unstable, the global error can grow without bound.\n\nOne way to study stability is to test a numerical method on the following **test equation**:\n\n$$\ny' = -\\lambda y, \\qquad y(0)=1, \\quad x \\geq 0, \\quad \\lambda > 0\n$$\n\nThe exact solution of the test equation is $y(x) = e^{-\\lambda x},$ which satisfies $y(x) \\to Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating [17592186120594 1063 17592186121007 17592186045417] [17592186121002 1064 "The **curvature** of a curve measures how much the curve \"bends\" at a given point. problems with periodic forcing functions.\n\nAs before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as\n\n$$\ny=y_c+y_p,\n$$\n\nwhere $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.\n\nThe main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:\n\n- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then\n\n- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.\n\nWhen $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$\n\nRecall that for an equation of the form $y''+\\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:\n\n- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.\n\n- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.\n\nFor example, consider the boundary value problem\n\n$$\ny''+5y=f(x)\n$$\n\non $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 [17592186199458 1064 "In this lesson, we discuss a concept analogous to *center of mass* that applies to rotating bodies.\n\nRecall that the *center of mass* of a plane lamina is defined as the point $(\\bar{x},\\bar{y})$ in the coordinate plane where the entire mass of the lamina could be concentrated to produce the same *total moment* about the coordinate axes as the original laminar. \n\nAnalogously, the **radius of gyration** of a plane lamina is the distance $R$ from an axis of rotation $L$ that the entire mass $M$ of the lamina would need to be concentrated to produce the same *moment of inertia* as the original lamina. \n\n![](images/c9/c9999bf30a93a857db731488739f0a640edc7b91de907cd772b777489a011fb8.png)\n\nTo derive an explicit formula for the radius of gyration, recall that the moment of inertia of a particle $P$ of mass $m$ at a distance of $r$ from an axis of rotation equals\n\n$$\nmr^2.\n$$\n\nSo, for a particle of mass $M$ at a distance of $R$ from the axis of [17592186281684 1070 17592186045487 17592186045417] [17592186281684 1071 "A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=3x,$ $x=1,$ $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis.
